parts.label: a
parts.text: Find \((f \circ g)(2)\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find an expression for \((g \circ f)(x)\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find \(f^{-1}(x)\), and hence find \(f^{-1}(11)\).

idea: \((f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x))\): apply \(g\) first, then \(f\). To find an inverse, write \(y = f(x)\), swap \(x\) and \(y\), and make \(y\) the subject.

stem: A delivery van uses \(F(d) = 0.08d + 1.5\) litres of fuel on a trip of \(d\) km (the extra 1.5 litres is for starting and idling). Fuel costs \(C(F) = 1.9F\) dollars for \(F\) litres.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the cost of the fuel for a 120 km trip.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find an expression for \((C \circ F)(d)\), and explain what it represents.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the inverse of \(C \circ F\), and hence find the length of trip that uses $30 of fuel.

idea: The output of \(F\) (litres) is the input of \(C\), so \(C \circ F\) turns a distance straight into a cost. Its inverse turns a cost back into a distance.

solution.label: b
solution.answer: \((C \circ F)(d) = 0.152d + 2.85\): the fuel cost, in dollars, of a trip of \(d\) km

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why \(f\) has an inverse on this domain, but not on all of \(\mathbb{R}\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find \(f^{-1}(x)\), and state its domain and range.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the value of \(x\) for which \(f(x) = f^{-1}(x)\).

idea: A function has an inverse only if it is one-to-one. The graphs of \(f\) and \(f^{-1}\) are reflections in \(y = x\), so for an increasing function they meet on that line.

solution.label: a
steps: For \(x \ge 2\) the function only increases, so each output comes from one input. On \(\mathbb{R}\), \(f(1) = f(3) = 2\).
solution.answer: It is one-to-one for \(x \ge 2\), but not on \(\mathbb{R}\)

solution.label: b
steps: The domain of \(f^{-1}\) is the range of \(f\), and the range of \(f^{-1}\) is the domain of \(f\).

stem: Let \(f(x) = 3e^{0.5x} - 2\), for \(x \in \mathbb{R}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the range of \(f\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find \(f^{-1}(x)\), and state its domain.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find \(f^{-1}(10)\), and check your answer.

idea: \(e^{0.5x}\) takes every positive value, so \(3e^{0.5x} - 2\) takes every value above \(-2\). The natural logarithm undoes \(e\): \(\ln e^{u} = u\).

stem: Let \(f(x) = \sqrt{x - 1}\), for \(x \ge 1\), and \(g(x) = x^{2} + 2x\), for \(x \in \mathbb{R}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find \((f \circ g)(3)\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the values of \(x\) for which \((f \circ g)(x)\) is defined.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find an expression for \((g \circ f)(x)\), and state its domain and range.

idea: \(f \circ g\) exists only where the output of \(g\) is in the domain of \(f\): here \(g(x) \ge 1\). For \(g \circ f\), the domain is that of \(f\).

solution.label: b
steps: The quadratic is positive outside its roots.

solution.label: c
steps: \(g(\sqrt{x - 1}) = (x - 1) + 2\sqrt{x - 1}\). Domain \(x \ge 1\). At \(x = 1\) the value is 0, and it increases from there.

stem: Let \(f(x) = \dfrac{2x + 1}{x - 2}\), for \(x \ne 2\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the equations of the asymptotes of the graph of \(f\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that \(f(f(x)) = x\), and hence write down \(f^{-1}(x)\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the values of \(x\) for which \(f(x) = x\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain, using a property of the graph, why your answers to part (c) are where the graph meets the line \(y = x\).

idea: A function with \(f(f(x)) = x\) is its own inverse, so its graph is symmetrical in the line \(y = x\).

solution.label: a
steps: The denominator is 0 at \(x = 2\). For large \(|x|\), \(f(x) \approx \dfrac{2x}{x} = 2\).

solution.label: d
steps: The graph of a self-inverse function is its own reflection in \(y = x\).
solution.answer: Points with \(f(x) = x\) lie on \(y = x\), the line of symmetry of the graph

stem: The graph of \(y = x^{2}\) is transformed to the graph of \(y = 3(x - 2)^{2} + 1\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a sequence of transformations that does this.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write down the coordinates of the vertex of the new graph.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the image of the point \((1, 1)\) on \(y = x^{2}\).

idea: \(y = af(x - h) + k\): a horizontal translation by \(h\), a vertical stretch by factor \(a\), then a vertical translation by \(k\).

solution.label: a
steps: \(x - 2\) inside: shift right. Multiply by 3: vertical stretch. Add 1: shift up.
solution.answer: A translation 2 units right, a vertical stretch with scale factor 3, then a translation 1 unit up

solution.label: b
steps: The vertex \((0, 0)\) moves right 2 and up 1; the stretch does not move it.

stem: The graph of \(y = f(x)\) is transformed to the graph of \(y = -f(2x) + 3\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the three transformations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the images of the points \((-4, 1)\), \((0, -2)\) and \((6, 5)\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write down the domain of the new function.

idea: \(f(2x)\) halves every \(x\)-coordinate; \(-f\) reflects in the \(x\)-axis; \(+3\) shifts up. A point \((x, y)\) goes to \(\left(\dfrac{x}{2}, -y + 3\right)\).

solution.label: a
steps: In order: \(f(2x)\), then multiply by \(-1\), then add 3.
solution.answer: A horizontal stretch with scale factor \(\dfrac{1}{2}\), a reflection in the \(x\)-axis, then a translation 3 units up

stem: The graph of \(y = e^{x}\) is transformed to the graph of \(y = 2e^{x - 1} - 3\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the transformations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote of the new graph.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the points where the new graph meets the axes.

idea: The asymptote \(y = 0\) of \(y = e^{x}\) is moved only by vertical translations; stretches and horizontal shifts leave it where it is.

solution.label: a
steps: \(x - 1\): right 1. Multiply by 2: vertical stretch. Subtract 3: down 3.
solution.answer: A translation 1 unit right, a vertical stretch with scale factor 2, then a translation 3 units down

stem: The graph of \(y = \sin x\) is transformed to the graph of \(y = g(x)\), where \(g(x) = 4\sin\left(2\left(x - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right) - 1\) and \(x\) is in radians.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the sequence of transformations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write down the period, and the greatest and least values of \(g\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the image of the point \(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}, 1\right)\), and hence the smallest positive \(x\) at which \(g\) has its greatest value.

idea: Inside the bracket, the stretch acts before the shift: \(\sin x \to \sin 2x \to \sin 2\left(x - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\). A maximum of \(\sin x\) moves to a maximum of \(g\).

solution.label: a
steps: \(\sin 2x\): horizontal stretch \(\dfrac{1}{2}\). Replace \(x\) by \(x - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\): shift right. Multiply by 4: vertical stretch. Subtract 1: shift down.
solution.answer: A horizontal stretch with scale factor \(\dfrac{1}{2}\), a translation \(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\) right, a vertical stretch with scale factor 4, and a translation 1 down

solution.label: c
steps: \(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}, 1\right)\) is a maximum of \(\sin x\), and the next one to the left, \(-\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\), goes to a negative \(x\).

stem: The graph of \(y = x^{2}\) is stretched vertically with scale factor \(a\) and then translated by \(\begin{pmatrix} h \\ k \end{pmatrix}\). The new graph passes through \((1, 5)\) and \((3, 5)\), and its least value is \(-3\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find \(h\), \(k\) and \(a\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The new graph is then reflected in the \(x\)-axis. Find the \(x\)-coordinates of the points where this last graph meets the \(x\)-axis.

idea: After the stretch and translation the graph is \(y = a(x - h)^{2} + k\). Two points at the same height are symmetrical about the axis \(x = h\), and the least value is \(k\).

solution.label: a
steps: The axis of symmetry is half way between \(x = 1\) and \(x = 3\): \(h = 2\). The least value is \(k = -3\).

solution.label: b
steps: Reflecting gives \(y = -8(x - 2)^{2} + 3\). It meets the \(x\)-axis where \((x - 2)^{2} = \dfrac{3}{8}\), so \(x = 2 \pm \sqrt{0.375} = 2 \pm 0.6123\ldots\)
(These are also where the unreflected graph meets the \(x\)-axis: a reflection in the \(x\)-axis does not move points on it.)

stem: A new lake is stocked with trout. The number of trout \(t\) years later is modelled by \(P(t) = \dfrac{2400}{1 + 11e^{-0.4t}}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of trout put into the lake.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write down the largest number of trout the lake can support, according to the model.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the number of trout after 5 years.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the time it takes for the number of trout to reach 1200.

idea: In the logistic model \(\dfrac{L}{1 + Ce^{-kt}}\), \(L\) is the carrying capacity, the starting value is \(\dfrac{L}{1 + C}\), and the population reaches \(\dfrac{L}{2}\) when \(Ce^{-kt} = 1\).

stem: A photo app takes \(t\) seconds to open an album of \(n\) photos, where \(t = 0.8\ln n + 1.2\), for \(n \ge 1\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the time to open an album of 1000 photos.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the largest album that opens in at most 7 seconds.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that doubling the number of photos always adds the same time, and find this time.

idea: Undo a natural logarithm with the exponential function: \(\ln n = u\) means \(n = e^{u}\). Since \(\ln 2n = \ln 2 + \ln n\), doubling \(n\) adds a fixed amount.

solution.label: b
steps: The number of photos is a whole number.

stem: The population of a city, \(P\) million, \(t\) years after 1 January 2020 is modelled by \(P = 1.2e^{0.018t}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the time it takes the population to double.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the year in which the population first reaches 2 million.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the equivalent annual percentage growth rate.

idea: With continuous growth \(e^{kt}\), the population is multiplied by \(e^{k}\) each year, which is an annual growth of \((e^{k} - 1) \times 100\) %.

solution.label: b
steps: \(1.2e^{0.018t} = 2\), so \(t = \dfrac{\ln(5/3)}{0.018} = 28.37\ldots\), which is during the 29th year after 2020.

stem: The number of listeners of a new podcast, \(N\), \(t\) weeks after its launch is modelled by \(N = \dfrac{5000}{1 + Ce^{-kt}}\). At launch it has 250 listeners, and after 4 weeks it has 1000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find \(C\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find \(k\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The number of listeners grows fastest when it is half of the carrying capacity. Using your unrounded value of \(k\), find when this happens.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the number of listeners after 10 weeks.

idea: Substitute the two known points in turn: \(t = 0\) gives \(C\), then \(t = 4\) gives an exponential equation for \(k\), solved with logarithms.

solution.label: d
solution.answer: 3610 listeners (3607 to the nearest whole number)

stem: A rumour spreads through a school of 1200 students. The number who have heard it \(t\) hours after 8 am is modelled by \(R = \dfrac{1200}{1 + Ce^{-kt}}\). At 8 am, 5 students have heard it; by 10 am, 60 have.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find \(C\) and \(k\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using your unrounded values, find the time of day, to the nearest minute, at which 90 % of the students have heard the rumour.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why an exponential model \(R = 5e^{kt}\) would not be suitable for the whole day.

idea: A logistic model levels off at its carrying capacity, here the whole school. An exponential model keeps growing, and would soon give more students than the school has.

solution.label: c
steps: For example, \(5e^{1.266 \times 10}\) is far more than 1200.
solution.answer: It grows without limit, but only 1200 students can hear the rumour

stem: The brightness of a variable star, \(B\), \(t\) days after observations start is modelled by \(B(t) = 0.8\sin(72(t - 1.5)) + 3.2\), where \(72(t - 1.5)\) is in degrees.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the amplitude and find the period.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the brightness when observations start.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the first time after \(t = 0\) at which the star is brightest, and its brightness then.

idea: In \(a\sin(b(t - c)) + d\): amplitude \(a\), period \(\dfrac{360}{b}\), and \(c\) is a horizontal shift. The sine is greatest when its angle is \(90^\circ\).

stem: A buoy rises and falls on the waves. Its height above the sea bed, \(h\) metres, \(t\) seconds after a recording starts is modelled by \(h = a\sin(b(t - c)) + d\), with \(a, b > 0\) and angles in degrees. Its greatest height is 2.6 m and its least is 0.4 m, one wave takes 5 seconds, and at \(t = 0.8\) the buoy is at its mean height and rising.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the height of the buoy at \(t = 3\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the length of time in each wave for which the buoy is more than 2 m above the sea bed.

idea: \(d\) is the mean of the greatest and least values, and \(a\) is half their difference. A sine curve passes through its mean height, rising, when its angle is 0, so \(t = c\) there.

stem: A patient's blood pressure, \(P\) mmHg, \(t\) seconds after a reading starts is modelled by \(P = 20\sin(450(t - 0.1)) + 100\), where the angle is in degrees.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the greatest and least blood pressure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the length of one heartbeat, and the heart rate in beats per minute.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the length of time in each heartbeat for which the pressure is above 110 mmHg, and the fraction of the beat this is.

idea: Each heartbeat is one period of the model. Within one period, \(\sin\theta > 0.5\) for \(30^\circ < \theta < 150^\circ\).

solution.label: c
solution.answer: 0.267 seconds, which is \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) of each beat

stem: A shop's monthly sales of sun cream, \(s\) units, \(t\) months after the start of the year are modelled by \(s = 40\sin(30(t - 2)) + 100\), for \(0 \le t \le 12\), where angles are in degrees. A second shop's sales are modelled by \(r = 30\sin(30(t - 5)) + 90\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the value of \(t\) at which the first shop's sales are greatest.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the value of \(h\), with \(0 \le h < 12\), for which \(s = 40\cos(30(t - h)) + 100\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the values of \(t\) for which the first shop sells more than the second.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one reason why the models might not fit next year.

idea: A cosine curve is a sine curve shifted so that it starts at its maximum: \(\cos\theta = \sin(\theta + 90^\circ)\). Compare two models by solving \(s = r\) with the calculator.

solution.label: b
steps: The cosine form has its maximum at \(t = h\), and the maximum is at \(t = 5\). Check: \(\cos(30(t - 5)) = \sin(30(t - 5) + 90) = \sin(30(t - 2))\).

solution.label: c
steps: Solve \(s = r\) with the calculator: \(t = 0.3864\ldots\) and \(t = 7.155\ldots\)

solution.label: d
steps: For example, a very hot or wet summer, or a price change.
solution.answer: Weather, prices or trends may differ from year to year

stem: A car park charges \(C(t)\) dollars for \(t\) hours, where \[C(t) = \begin{cases} 3t, & 0 < t \le 2 \\ 6 + 2(t - 2), & 2 < t \le 6 \\ 14, & t > 6. \end{cases}\]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the time for which a driver pays $10.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the model is continuous at \(t = 6\).

idea: Use the rule for the interval that contains \(t\). Check which piece a given cost belongs to before solving.

solution.label: b
steps: $10 is between \(C(2) = 6\) and \(C(6) = 14\), so use the middle rule: \(6 + 2(t - 2) = 10\).

stem: Let \(f(x) = \begin{cases} x^{2} + 1, & x < 2 \\ kx - 3, & x \ge 2. \end{cases}\)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the value of \(k\) for which the graph of \(f\) has no break at \(x = 2\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: For this value of \(k\), solve \(f(x) = 10\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the range of \(f\).

idea: The two pieces join if they give the same value at \(x = 2\). An equation with a piecewise function is solved piece by piece, keeping only solutions in each piece's own interval.

solution.label: c
steps: The first piece takes every value from 1 upwards (its least value is 1 at \(x = 0\)); the second gives values from 5 upwards.

stem: A 1500 m\(^{3}\) swimming pool is filled using two pipes. For the first 2 hours the water comes in at 300 m\(^{3}\) per hour; then one pipe is closed and the water comes in at 180 m\(^{3}\) per hour until the pool is full.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down a piecewise model for the volume \(V\) after \(t\) hours.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the time it takes to fill the pool.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the time at which the pool holds 1000 m\(^{3}\), in hours and minutes.

idea: Each piece is linear, with gradient equal to the rate of flow. The second piece starts from the volume reached at the end of the first.

solution.label: a
solution.answer: \(V = 300t\) for \(0 \le t \le 2\); \(V = 600 + 180(t - 2)\) for \(2 < t \le 7\) (when the pool is full)

stem: The profile of a skateboard ramp is modelled by \(y = \begin{cases} ax^{2}, & 0 \le x \le 4 \\ 2x - 4, & 4 < x \le 10, \end{cases}\) where \(x\) and \(y\) are in metres and the two pieces join.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find \(a\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the height of the ramp at \(x = 3\) and at \(x = 7\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the two points of the profile at which the height is 2 m and 13 m.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the range of the function.

idea: The pieces join at \(x = 4\), so they give the same height there. To find \(x\) from a height, first decide which piece the height lies on.

solution.label: c
steps: Height 2 is below 4, so it is on the curve: \(0.25x^{2} = 2\), \(x = \sqrt{8} = 2.828\ldots\)
Height 13 is above 4, so it is on the line: \(2x - 4 = 13\), \(x = 8.5\).

solution.label: d
steps: From 0 at \(x = 0\) up to \(2 \times 10 - 4 = 16\) at \(x = 10\), always increasing.

stem: The masses of four animals are: mouse 0.02 kg, adult human 70 kg, elephant 6000 kg, blue whale 150 000 kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find \(\log_{10}\) of each mass, correct to two decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a logarithmic scale is useful for showing these masses on one axis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the difference of the unrounded logarithms of the two masses to find how many times heavier the blue whale is than the mouse.

idea: On a logarithmic scale, equal steps mean equal multiplying factors. The difference of two logarithms is the logarithm of their ratio.

solution.label: b
steps: The masses go from hundredths to hundreds of thousands; on an ordinary scale the mouse and the human would be at the same point.
solution.answer: The values cover many powers of 10, which a log scale spreads evenly

stem: A new video channel records its number of subscribers, \(y\) thousand, at the end of each of its first eight weeks, \(x\).

\[\def\arraystretch{1.4}\begin{array}{|c|c|}\hline \text{Week, x} & \text{Subscribers, y (thousands)} \\ \hline 1 & 4.8 \\ \hline 2 & 6.5 \\ \hline 3 & 9.6 \\ \hline 4 & 13.0 \\ \hline 5 & 19.1 \\ \hline 6 & 27.0 \\ \hline 7 & 38.5 \\ \hline 8 & 54.0 \\ \hline \end{array}\]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the equation of the regression line of \(\ln y\) on \(x\), and the correlation coefficient for \(\ln y\) and \(x\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence write the model in the form \(y = ae^{bx}\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the model to estimate the number of subscribers at the end of week 10.

idea: If \(y = ae^{bx}\), then \(\ln y = \ln a + bx\): a straight line when \(\ln y\) is plotted against \(x\). The gradient is \(b\) and the intercept is \(\ln a\).

solution.label: a
steps: Enter \(x\) and \(\ln y\) in the calculator: gradient \(0.3490\ldots\), intercept \(1.198\ldots\), \(r = 0.9997\ldots\)

stem: The moons of a planet have orbital radius \(r\) (in units of 100 000 km) and orbital period \(T\) days.
\[\def\arraystretch{1.4}\begin{array}{|c|c|}\hline \text{Radius, r} & \text{Period, T (days)} \\ \hline 1 & 1.2 \\ \hline 2 & 3.4 \\ \hline 4 & 9.6 \\ \hline 8 & 27.1 \\ \hline \end{array}\]
A model of the form \(T = ar^{b}\) is proposed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that \(\ln T = \ln a + b\ln r\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the regression line of \(\ln T\) on \(\ln r\), and hence find \(a\) and \(b\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Estimate the period of a moon with orbital radius 600 000 km.

idea: Taking logarithms of a power model gives a straight line in \(\ln r\) and \(\ln T\): the gradient is the power \(b\) and the intercept is \(\ln a\).

solution.label: a
steps: \(\ln T = \ln(ar^{b}) = \ln a + \ln r^{b} = \ln a + b\ln r\)

solution.label: b
steps: Regression of \(\ln T\) on \(\ln r\): gradient \(1.498\ldots\), intercept \(0.1834\ldots\)

stem: An experiment gives these values of \(x\) and \(y\).

\[\def\arraystretch{1.4}\begin{array}{|c|c|}\hline \text{x} & \text{y} \\ \hline 1 & 3.0 \\ \hline 2 & 5.2 \\ \hline 4 & 9.1 \\ \hline 6 & 12.5 \\ \hline 8 & 15.8 \\ \hline 10 & 18.9 \\ \hline \end{array}\]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the correlation coefficient between \(\ln y\) and \(x\), and between \(\ln y\) and \(\ln x\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence state whether an exponential model \(y = ae^{bx}\) or a power model \(y = ax^{b}\) fits the data better.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the better model, and use it to estimate \(y\) when \(x = 15\).

idea: An exponential model is linear in \((x, \ln y)\); a power model is linear in \((\ln x, \ln y)\). The model whose transformed data are closest to a straight line fits better.

solution.label: a
steps: From the calculator: \(\ln y\) against \(x\): \(r = 0.9565\ldots\); \(\ln y\) against \(\ln x\): \(r = 0.99999\ldots\)

solution.label: b
steps: The second is much closer to 1.

solution.label: c
steps: Regression of \(\ln y\) on \(\ln x\): gradient \(0.7993\ldots\), intercept \(1.097\ldots\), so \(a = e^{1.097\ldots} = 2.995\ldots\)

stem: Ecologists find that the number of plant species \(S\) on an island and the island's area \(A\) km\(^{2}\) fit the line \(\log_{10} S = 0.25\log_{10} A + 1.1\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that \(S = kA^{0.25}\), and find \(k\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Estimate the number of species on an island of area 10 000 km\(^{2}\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using the unrounded value of \(k\), estimate the area of an island with 50 species.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the factor by which \(S\) is multiplied when the area is doubled.

idea: Undo the logarithms by raising 10 to each side: \(10^{\log_{10} S} = S\). In a power law, multiplying \(A\) by a factor multiplies \(S\) by that factor to the power 0.25.

stem: The value of a car, \(V\) dollars, \(t\) years after it is bought is recorded. A dealer expects the value to approach a scrap value of $1500, using the model \(V = 1500 + Ae^{kt}\).

\[\def\arraystretch{1.4}\begin{array}{|c|c|}\hline \text{Age, t (years)} & \text{Value, V (dollars)} \\ \hline 0 & 24000 \\ \hline 1 & 19500 \\ \hline 2 & 15800 \\ \hline 3 & 12900 \\ \hline 4 & 10600 \\ \hline 5 & 8800 \\ \hline 6 & 7350 \\ \hline \end{array}\]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that \(\ln(V - 1500) = \ln A + kt\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the regression line of \(\ln(V - 1500)\) on \(t\), and hence find \(A\) and \(k\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the age at which the model predicts the car's value falls to $5000.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why a model of the form \(V = Ae^{kt}\), without the 1500, would be less suitable in the long term.

idea: Subtract the scrap value first: \(V - 1500\) is a pure exponential, so its logarithm is linear in \(t\).

solution.label: d
steps: Without the 1500 the value would fall towards $0.
solution.answer: It would predict the car becomes worthless, but a car always has some scrap value
